o: The main sensory nucleus lies ventral to the superior cerebellar peduncle

It lies in the upper pons, lateral to the motor nucleus and ventral to the superior cerebellar peduncle.
It mediates touch. (Last's p. 631)
The trigeminal motor nucleus lies in the midline beneath the floor of the fourth ventricle

It is branchial, so it lies off centre, deep beneath the floor.
Somatic motor nuclei are the ones near the midline. (Last's p. 631)
The spinal nucleus is continuous with the gelatinous substance as far as C3

Last's: continuous at its lower end with the gelatinous substance "as far as the third cervical segment".
It mediates pain and temperature. (Last's p. 631)
Last's accepts the "upside-down" ophthalmic-lowest arrangement in the spinal nucleus

Last's says clinical observations indicate an "onion-skin" pattern working backwards from the mouth.
The upside-down scheme is "usually stated". (Last's p. 631)

questions.s: Concerning the trigeminal roots and cave (Last's):
o: The motor root emerges slightly cranial and medial to the sensory root
The large sensory root attaches well lateral and just above centre; the motor root emerges separately, cranial and medial. (Last's p. 631)
The dural sheath fuses with the pia at the anterior border of the ganglion

It fuses with the pia halfway along the ganglion, the anterior extremity of the cave.
So the posterior half of the ganglion and both roots are bathed in CSF. (Last's p. 631)
The motor root passes beneath the ganglion to join V3 at the foramen ovale
The motor root remains separate from the ganglion and joins the mandibular division at the foramen ovale. (Last's p. 631, 633)
The trigeminal cave lies medial to the dural split that encloses the cavernous sinus
The sheath peels apart the floor dura just lateral to where the same layers enclose the cavernous sinus. (Last's p. 631)
It is the nerve of the frontonasal process

Last's: V1 is the nerve of the frontonasal process.
V2 is the nerve of the maxillary process. (Last's p. 631-2)
It runs in the lateral wall of the cavernous sinus above the trochlear nerve

It runs below the trochlear nerve.
It picks up sympathetic fibres for dilator pupillae there. (Last's p. 631)
Its tentorial nerves supply all supratentorial dura except that in the bony floor of the middle fossa

They arise at the anterior end of the cavernous sinus.
The middle fossa floor is supplied by meningeal branches of V2 and V3. (Last's p. 631)
The frontal nerve passes through the superior orbital fissure within the tendinous ring

It traverses the fissure just lateral to the ring, between lacrimal and trochlear nerves.
Nasociliary enters the ring between the divisions of III. (Last's p. 631-2)
The supratrochlear nerve scarcely extends beyond the hairline

It supplies a narrow strip of forehead beside the midline.
The supraorbital supplies the frontal scalp to the vertex. (Last's p. 632)
The supraorbital nerve supplies the whole forehead including the central strip

It supplies all the forehead except a central strip.
It also supplies the frontal sinus. (Last's p. 632)
The lacrimal nerve supplies both surfaces of the lateral upper conjunctiva
It supplies a fingertip area of skin at the lateral end of the upper lid and both conjunctival surfaces. (Last's p. 631)
The nasociliary nerve runs below the medial rectus on the medial orbital wall

It runs below the superior oblique and above the medial rectus.
It then enters the anterior ethmoidal foramen. (Last's p. 632)
It changes its name twice

It becomes the anterior ethmoidal and then the external nasal nerve.
It makes a brief appearance in the anterior cranial fossa. (Last's p. 632)
The posterior ethmoidal nerve supplies the posterior nasal cavity

It supplies the posterior ethmoidal cells and sphenoidal sinus but does not reach the nasal cavity.
It is often very small or absent. (Last's p. 632)
The infratrochlear nerve arises just before the nasociliary enters the anterior ethmoidal foramen

The posterior ethmoidal arises proximal to it.
The infratrochlear ends on the bridge of the nose. (Last's p. 632)
The short ciliary nerves supply the conjunctiva

Both long and short ciliary nerves are sensory to the eye including the cornea, but not the conjunctiva.
There are 8–10 short ciliary nerves. (Last's p. 632)
Its lateral cavernous wall fuses with outer dura at the margin of foramen rotundum
This directs V2 through the foramen into the upper pterygopalatine fossa. (Last's p. 632)
It turns medially for about a centimetre in the inferior orbital fissure
It turns laterally for a centimetre or so, becoming the infraorbital nerve. (Last's p. 632)
Its middle meningeal nerve supplies the dura of the anterior half of the middle fossa
V3's nervus spinosus supplies the posterior half. (Last's p. 632-3)
The nasopalatine nerve supplies the posterosuperior quadrant of the septum

It supplies the posteroinferior half of the septum.
The posterior superior medial nasal nerve supplies the posterosuperior part. (Last's p. 632-3)
The greater palatine nerve runs between the palatine perpendicular plate and the maxilla

It supplies the posteroinferior lateral nasal wall, nasal floor and maxillary sinus.
It supplies all the hard palate except behind the incisors. (Last's p. 633)
The lesser palatine nerves supply only the oral surface of the soft palate
They supply both surfaces of the soft palate and the tonsil. (Last's p. 633)
The pharyngeal branch supplies the nasopharynx down to the auditory tube opening

It passes back through the palatovaginal canal.
It may supply part of the tubal mucosa. (Last's p. 633)
The zygomaticofacial nerve supplies the hairless skin of the temple

The zygomaticotemporal nerve supplies the hairless temple skin.
The zygomaticofacial supplies the skin over the zygomatic bone. (Last's p. 633)
One branch of the posterior superior alveolar nerve stays outside the maxilla

The third branch pierces buccinator and supplies the vestibular gum of the molars.
The other two enter the maxilla above the tuberosity. (Last's p. 633)
The posterior superior alveolar nerve supplies all roots of the first molar
It spares the anterior buccal root of the first molar, which the middle superior alveolar supplies. (Last's p. 633)
The anterior superior alveolar nerve supplies the nasolacrimal duct region

It reaches the anterior inferior quadrant of the lateral nasal wall including the nasolacrimal duct, and ends on the septum.
It supplies the canine and incisors. (Last's p. 633)
The middle superior alveolar nerve arises in the infraorbital canal
It arises in the infraorbital groove; the anterior superior alveolar arises in the canal. (Last's p. 633)

questions.s: Concerning the infraorbital nerve on the face (Last's):
o: It emerges between levator labii superioris and levator anguli oris

Last's places it between these two muscles.
It communicates with facial nerve branches for proprioception. (Last's p. 633)
Its labial branches supply the gum only as far as the canine

They supply the gum from the midline to include the second premolar.
They supply the whole upper lip. (Last's p. 633)
Its palpebral branches supply both surfaces of the lower lid conjunctiva
They supply the skin of the lower lid and both conjunctival surfaces. (Last's p. 633)
Its communications with the facial nerve carry motor fibres to the facial muscles
They are for the proprioceptive supply of nearby facial muscles. (Last's p. 633)
It enters the infratemporal fossa between the upper head of lateral pterygoid and tensor palati

Tensor palati lies on the side wall of the nasopharynx.
It divides after 4 or 5 mm. (Last's p. 633)
The nervus spinosus always passes through the foramen spinosum
It passes up through the foramen ovale, sometimes through the foramen spinosum. (Last's p. 633)
The nervus spinosus supplies the mastoid air cells

It passes between squamous and petrous temporal bone to the mastoid antrum and air cells.
It is the nerve of the first pharyngeal pouch. (Last's p. 633)
The nervus spinosus supplies the dura of the anterior half of the middle fossa

It supplies the posterior half.
The middle meningeal branch of V2 supplies the anterior half. (Last's p. 632-3)

questions.s: Anterior branches of the mandibular nerve (Last's):
o: The deep temporal nerves pass above the upper head of lateral pterygoid

They turn above the infratemporal crest to sink into temporalis.
So does the nerve to masseter. (Last's p. 634)
There are two nerves to the medial pterygoid in the anterior group
The anterior group has two nerves to the lateral pterygoid; the nerve to medial pterygoid arises from the trunk. (Last's p. 634)
The buccal nerve may carry a middle temporal nerve

It sometimes carries a middle temporal nerve to the deep surface of temporalis.
It passes between the two heads of lateral pterygoid. (Last's p. 634)
The buccal nerve carries secretomotor fibres from the submandibular ganglion
It carries otic ganglion fibres for the molar and buccal glands. (Last's p. 634)

questions.s: Posterior branches of the mandibular nerve (Last's):
o: The auriculotemporal nerve's two roots encircle the middle meningeal artery

They pass back around the artery.
It then passes deep to the neck of the mandible. (Last's p. 634)
The auricular branch of the auriculotemporal nerve supplies the auricle below the meatus
It supplies the meatus and the external auricle above it. (Last's p. 634)
The incisive branch overlaps to the opposite central incisor
It supplies the canine and both incisors and overlaps to the opposite central incisor. (Last's p. 634)
The nerve to mylohyoid lies between mylohyoid and the posterior belly of digastric
It runs between mylohyoid and the anterior belly, supplying both. (Last's p. 634)
It is joined by the chorda tympani deep to the lower border of lateral pterygoid

About 2 cm below the base of the skull.
It then curves down on medial pterygoid. (Last's p. 634)
It passes over the upper border of the superior constrictor

It passes under the free lower border of the superior constrictor.
It then runs above mylohyoid in the mouth. (Last's p. 634)
It grooves the lingual plate just below the last molar
It gives a gingival branch to the lingual gum here. (Last's p. 634)
It alone supplies all the mucous membrane of the floor of the mouth
Last's: "The lingual nerve and no other supplies all the mucous membrane of the floor of the mouth." (Last's p. 634)
It turns upwards between the anterior inferior cerebellar artery and the pons

It enters the pontine cistern and runs up between AICA and the pons.
It pierces arachnoid and dura on the clivus. (Last's p. 635)
It pierces the dura on the clivus below the level of the jugular tubercle
It pierces the dura above the level of the jugular tubercle. (Last's p. 635)
It enters the inferior petrosal sinus at the apex of the petrous bone
It then bends forwards under the petroclinoid ligament into the cavernous sinus. (Last's p. 635)
It enters the tendinous ring above the superior division of the oculomotor nerve

It enters the ring below the inferior division of III.
It enters the ocular surface of lateral rectus a third of the way along. (Last's p. 635)
Last's suggests it should perhaps be called the intermediofacial nerve

To emphasise that the nervus intermedius is part of it.
"Sensory root" is not appropriate, as it also has visceral efferents. (Last's p. 635)
Its sensory fibres from the external ear end in the nucleus of the tractus solitarius

Those few skin fibres, with cell bodies in the geniculate ganglion, pass to trigeminal nuclei.
Taste fibres go to the tractus solitarius. (Last's p. 635)
In the internal acoustic meatus the nervus intermedius lies between the facial and vestibulocochlear nerves

The main facial nerve lies on the upper surface of VIII with the intermedius between.
The facial nerve enters the anterosuperior quadrant. (Last's p. 635)
The facial muscles receive proprioception through the facial nerve

Their proprioceptive supply comes from cutaneous trigeminal branches in the overlying skin.
The nerve leaves the stylomastoid foramen purely branchial motor. (Last's p. 635)

questions.s: The facial nerve in the temporal bone (Last's):
o: It runs laterally above the vestibule of the internal ear
The two parts share a common tube of arachnoid and dura, then fuse into one trunk. (Last's p. 635)
In the medial wall of the middle ear it runs below the promontory
It runs above the promontory, just below the bulge of the lateral semicircular canal. (Last's p. 635)
It curves down behind the middle ear deep to the aditus
It then passes vertically down the facial canal. (Last's p. 635)
At the geniculum it makes a sharp anterior bend

The geniculum is a sharp posterior bend near the middle ear.
It is distended by the geniculate ganglion. (Last's p. 635)
The greater petrosal nerve passes beneath the trigeminal ganglion in Meckel's cave
It slants forward between the dural layers to the foramen lacerum. (Last's p. 636)
The deep petrosal nerve's cell bodies are in the inferior cervical ganglion

They are in the superior cervical ganglion.
It peels off the internal carotid plexus. (Last's p. 636)
Taste fibres pass through the pterygopalatine ganglion without relaying
So do the sympathetic and maxillary sensory fibres; only secretomotor fibres relay. (Last's p. 636)
Last's lists four territories of the pterygopalatine ganglion
Last's lists five: nasal septum, lateral nasal wall, paranasal sinuses, hard and soft palates, and nasopharynx. (Last's p. 636)
Tympanic branches of VII can reach the skin of the external meatus and pinna

They trespass into auriculotemporal territory, so geniculate herpes produces vesicles there.
Their cell bodies are in the geniculate ganglion. (Last's p. 636)
The nerve to stapedius reaches the muscle through the pyramid's opening without a canal
It is given off in the facial canal and reaches the muscle by a minute canaliculus. (Last's p. 636)
The chorda tympani crosses the pars flaccida and the neck of the malleus

It is draped over by mucous membrane.
It leaves through the anterior wall of the middle ear. (Last's p. 636)
The posterior auricular nerve supplies the frontal belly of occipitofrontalis
It supplies the occipital belly. (Last's p. 636)
It pierces dura and arachnoid at the anteroinferior quadrant of the internal meatus
Its fibres join in a spiral pattern at the base of the modiolus. (Last's p. 636)
The spiral ganglion lies in the modiolus

Its cell bodies lie in the base of the bony spiral lamina.
Central processes run along the modiolus. (Last's p. 636)
Some cochlear fibres ascend in the lateral lemniscus of their own side
Not all cross, so representation is largely bilateral. (Last's p. 637)
The VIII nerve enters the middle cerebellar peduncle
It enters the inferior cerebellar peduncle at the lower border of the pons. (Last's p. 637)
The posterior semicircular duct's nerve emerges through the foramen singulare
It lies alongside the lower division from the saccule. (Last's p. 637)
The utricular nerve emerges through the posteroinferior quadrant of the fundus

The utricle with the anterior and lateral ducts uses the posterosuperior quadrant.
The saccule uses the posteroinferior quadrant. (Last's p. 637)
Vestibular ganglia lie within the internal acoustic meatus
The upper and lower divisions are distended there by the first-order cell bodies. (Last's p. 637)
Last's describes vestibular cortical connexions via the lateral geniculate body
Last's says cortical connexions appear to run by bilateral thalamic relay via the medial geniculate body. (Last's p. 637)
The inferior salivary nucleus lies in the lowest pons rostral to the dorsal vagal nucleus
It supplies the parotid via the lesser petrosal nerve and otic ganglion. (Last's p. 637)
Its taste fibres end in the nucleus of the tractus solitarius in the upper medulla

Last's here says the lower medulla for IX's taste and carotid afferents.
General sensation goes to the trigeminal nuclei. (Last's p. 637)
In the jugular foramen it lies lateral to the inferior petrosal sinus

Both are separated from X and XI by a septum of fibrous dura.
It enters the anterior compartment. (Last's p. 637)
Its superior ganglion is larger than the inferior
The superior ganglion is a small detached part of the elongated inferior ganglion. (Last's p. 637)
The lesser petrosal nerve may pass through a petrosal foramen instead of the foramen ovale

It runs through the foramen ovale (or petrosal foramen) to the otic ganglion.
It arises from the tympanic plexus. (Last's p. 638)
The tonsillar branch is motor to palatoglossus

It provides afferent fibres for the tonsillar mucosa.
The only muscular branch is to stylopharyngeus. (Last's p. 638)
The lingual branch carries a few secretomotor fibres for lingual glands
It is mainly sensory to the posterior tongue. (Last's p. 638)
The carotid sinus nerve connects mainly with the cerebellum
It provides vital connexions with autonomic cell groups in the reticular formation. (Last's p. 638)
Its rootlets leave below those of IX between olive and inferior cerebellar peduncle
The nerve crosses the basiocciput behind the jugular tubercle, below IX and above XI. (Last's p. 638)
In the jugular foramen it lies lateral to the accessory nerve

It lies medial to the accessory, just in front of the jugular bulb.
Both use the middle compartment. (Last's p. 638)
Its superior ganglion has cell bodies only for meningeal and auricular branches
The inferior ganglion lodges all its other sensory cell bodies. (Last's p. 638)
The accessory nerve joins the vagus at the superior vagal ganglion

It gives all its nucleus ambiguus fibres to the vagus at the inferior ganglion.
Last's likens this to a spinal motor root joining distal to the ganglion. (Last's p. 638)
The pharyngeal branch passes between the internal and external carotid arteries
It carries motor and sensory fibres to the pharyngeal plexus. (Last's p. 638)
The superior laryngeal branch runs superficial to the carotid arteries
It runs deep to the carotids before dividing. (Last's p. 638)
The vagus is sensory to the oesophagus, trachea and lungs

From abdominal viscera, pain runs with sympathetic fibres.
Vagal gut branches do not carry pain. (Last's p. 638)
The vagal trunks supply the stomach by branches arising in the greater omentum
Their branches arise in the lesser omentum. (Last's p. 638)
Its spinal nucleus lies mainly in C2, C3 and C4
It spans the upper five or six cervical segments, mainly 2, 3 and 4. (Last's p. 638)
Its spinal roots emerge in front of the denticulate ligament

They emerge from the lateral cord behind the denticulate ligament.
The trunk passes over the upper tooth of the ligament. (Last's p. 638)
It passes through the lateral part of the middle compartment of the jugular foramen
The vagus lies medial to it. (Last's p. 638)
In the neck it lies on the internal carotid artery over the atlas
It lies on the internal jugular vein over the lateral mass of the atlas. (Last's p. 638)
Its exit from the skull is medial and posterior to the jugular foramen
So it spirals down and forward with a lateral convexity, becoming more superficial. (Last's p. 639)
Below the posterior belly of digastric it lies on the internal carotid, external carotid and lingual arteries

It lies on the occipital, external carotid and lingual arteries.
It is covered only by the facial vein beneath the investing fascia. (Last's p. 639)
Its spiral course is the migration path of the suboccipital myotomes

These form the tongue muscles.
It curves outside the arteries but deep to the veins. (Last's p. 639)
It runs below the greater horn of the hyoid as it splits into its branches

It runs above the greater horn.
It supplies all tongue muscles except palatoglossus. (Last's p. 639)

questions.s: Branches carried by the hypoglossal nerve (Last's):
o: Its meningeal branch supplies a ring of dura beyond the margin of the foramen magnum
It is very small. (Last's p. 639)
Sternothyroid is supplied by C1, C2 and C3
Sternothyroid is C2 and C3; sternohyoid and omohyoid are C1, 2, 3. (Last's p. 640)
The nerve to geniohyoid carries the last of the C1 fibres

It is given off in the mouth, above mylohyoid.
The nerve to thyrohyoid (C1) arises as XII lies on the lingual artery. (Last's p. 640)
The ansa cervicalis lies embedded in the posterior wall of the carotid sheath
It lies on the IJV under sternocleidomastoid, embedded in the anterior wall of the sheath. (Last's p. 639)
The cranial nerves most often affected by trauma include the sixth

Last's lists I, II, III, VI and VII.
Tumours, ischaemia and aneurysms are other usual causes. (Last's p. 640)
Olfactory hallucinations arise from the anterior perforated substance
They arise from the uncus, the cortical centre for smell. (Last's p. 640)
The upper visual field is represented below the calcarine sulcus
It is also represented in the lateral part of the lateral geniculate body. (Last's p. 640)
Macular sparing occurs because the occipital tip is supplied by the anterior choroidal artery

Last's says the tip is supplied by the middle cerebral artery.
So PCA occlusion spares macular vision. (Last's p. 640)
Clinically the commonest lesions are at the chiasma and in the optic radiation
Last's names sites 2 and 4 as commonest. (Last's p. 640)
A left temporal lobe abscess gives a right lower quadrantic defect
It damages the lower fibres of the left radiation, giving a right upper quadrantanopia. (Last's p. 640)
Lesions of the upper fibres of the optic radiation are in practice very rare
They come from parietal lesions and give a lower quadrantanopia. (Last's p. 640)
Traumatic damage to the left occipital tip gives a left macular defect
It gives a right homonymous (macular) defect. (Last's p. 640)
In trochlear palsy the head is tilted towards the opposite shoulder

This compensates for extorsion.
The eye cannot look down fully when turned in. (Last's p. 641)
Ptosis with a small pupil suggests an oculomotor lesion
Ptosis with a large pupil suggests III; with a small pupil, Horner's syndrome. (Last's p. 641)
Trigeminal neuralgia rarely involves the ophthalmic division
It usually affects maxillary and/or mandibular territory, and rarely the whole of a division. (Last's p. 641)
In mandibular trigeminal neuralgia pain spreads along the angle of the mandible

The angle is supplied by the great auricular nerve, so pain is not felt there.
It runs from the mouth to the ear and temple. (Last's p. 641)
The ophthalmic territory reaches back to a line drawn upwards from the ears

It stretches from the tip of the nose to the vertex.
Nose-tip vesicles warn of corneal involvement. (Last's p. 641)
The afferent limb of the corneal reflex runs in the lacrimal nerve

It depends on ciliary branches of the nasociliary nerve.
Its loss is often the first sign of a V1 lesion. (Last's p. 641)
Bell's palsy is thought to involve swelling just before the stylomastoid foramen
It is probably a viral infection in the facial canal. (Last's p. 641)
Emotional facial movements are lost in supranuclear facial lesions

Emotional movements such as smiling are still possible.
Voluntary lower face movement is lost. (Last's p. 641)
In Weber's test with conduction deafness the sound is louder in the deaf ear
With nerve deafness it is louder in the good ear. (Last's p. 641-2)
In Rinne's test with conduction deafness the sound is heard again at the meatus
It is not heard again; it is with a normal ear or nerve deafness. (Last's p. 642)
Cool water irrigation causes nystagmus to the opposite side

Warm water causes nystagmus to the same side.
The slow phase follows the endolymph. (Last's p. 642)
Vestibular nerve damage gives an exaggerated response only in one head position
Inner ear disease gives the position-specific response; nerve damage gives it in any position. (Last's p. 642)
Malignant disease is the commonest cause of recurrent laryngeal palsy

About 25% malignant and 20% surgical.
Left palsies are much commoner. (Last's p. 642)
In an incomplete recurrent laryngeal lesion the cord lies abducted

It lies adducted; abduction seems lost first.
Complete paralysis gives an intermediate position. (Last's p. 642)
With a unilateral palatal paralysis the uvula is pulled towards the normal side
The unaffected side rises further. (Last's p. 642)
A posterior triangle accessory lesion always paralyses the whole trapezius

It paralyses the upper part, but not always the lower part.
A higher lesion also paralyses sternocleidomastoid. (Last's p. 642)
